content: Kunjin virus (KUNV) is a zoonotic virus that belongs to the family Flaviviridae and the genus Flavivirus. It is a subtype of the West Nile virus and is endemic to the Oceania region. The virus was first isolated in 1960 from mosquitoes of the species Culex annulirostris in Australia. Its name, Kunjin virus, originates from an Aboriginal clan residing near the Mitchell River in northern Queensland, close to the location where the virus was initially identified in Kowanyama. Kunjin virus is classified as an arbovirus, meaning it is transmitted by arthropods, specifically mosquitoes. It is part of the Japanese encephalitis serological complex. Antigenically and genetically, it is highly similar to the West Nile virus. In 1999, it was reclassified as a subtype of the West Nile virus. The virus has a positive-sense, single-stranded RNA genome consisting of 10,644 nucleotides. Infection with Kunjin virus is often asymptomatic. However, in some cases, it can result in either encephalitic or non-encephalitic disease. Non-encephalitic Kunjin virus disease may present with symptoms such as acute febrile illness, headache, joint pain (arthralgia), muscle pain (myalgia), fatigue, and rash. In contrast, Kunjin virus encephalitis manifests as acute febrile meningoencephalitis. Both forms of the disease are generally milder compared to illnesses caused by the West Nile virus or the Murray Valley encephalitis virus. The virus is transmitted primarily by mosquito vectors, particularly Culex annulirostris. These mosquitoes transmit the virus to waterbird reservoir hosts, with the nankeen night heron being a notable example. The virus can also infect horses and humans. While the virus has been isolated in mosquitoes in Southeast Asia, human cases have only been reported in Australia. It is found throughout Australia, with higher prevalence in areas near wetlands and rivers. Control of Kunjin virus is similar to the management of other mosquito-borne diseases. Preventive measures include the use of insect repellents, wearing long-sleeved clothing, and avoiding areas with high mosquito activity. Government-led habitat control efforts may involve reducing standing water to limit mosquito breeding and applying insecticides. Currently, there is no vaccine available for Kunjin virus. In 2005, researchers at the Queensland Institute of Medical Research and the University of Queensland discovered that modified Kunjin virus particles, when injected into mice, could deliver a gene targeting cancer cells to the immune system. This research holds potential for the development of vaccines for cancer and HIV.
